title: Episode 46: Bleeding Kansas and John Brown's Raid on Pottawatomie
description:
In the 1850s, the Kansas Territory became a bloody ideological battleground over slavery. Pro-slavery 'Border Ruffians' from Missouri clashed with New England abolitionist Free-Staters armed with 'Beecher's Bibles.' Following the sack of Lawrence, fiery abolitionist John Brown led a midnight retaliatory strike along Pottawatomie Creek, executing five pro-slavery settlers with broadswords.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Seven years before the first cannon fired at Fort Sumter, the American Civil War began in the rolling prairie grass of the Kansas Territory. In eighteen fifty-four, the passage of the Kansas-Nebraska Act repealed the Missouri Compromise, declaring that whether Kansas entered the Union as a free or slave state would be decided by 'popular sovereignty'—the vote of the settlers themselves. Almost overnight, Kansas became a violent magnet for fanaticism. Abolitionist societies in Boston raised funds to ship hundreds of settlers armed with Sharps rifles shipped in crates labeled 'Bibles,' while thousands of heavily armed pro-slavery vigilantes from Missouri known as 'Border Ruffians' crossed the river to hijack elections and terrorize free-soil towns. In May eighteen fifty-six, the violence culminated in a midnight massacre along Pottawatomie Creek, led by an uncompromising, Old Testament-style zealot named John Brown. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE FIRESTORM OF POPULAR SOVEREIGNTY
In May eighteen fifty-four, President Franklin Pierce signed the Kansas-Nebraska Act into law, an explosive piece of legislation authored by Illinois Senator Stephen A. Douglas. The act organized the two vast territories of Kansas and Nebraska, but it contained a fateful political bargain: it repealed the historic Missouri Compromise line of eighteen twenty, which had banned slavery north of thirty-six degrees thirty minutes latitude. Instead, Douglas introduced the doctrine of 'popular sovereignty,' allowing the white male settlers of each territory to decide for themselves whether to legalize slavery. Douglas naively believed this democratic mechanism would remove the slavery question from national politics; instead, it transformed the Kansas prairie into a ferocious, zero-sum civil war. Northern abolitionists and Southern slaveholders both understood that whichever side controlled Kansas would control two seats in the United States Senate and permanently tilt the balance of national power. In Boston, wealthy abolitionists formed the New England Emigrant Aid Company, raising hundreds of thousands of dollars to transport thousands of free-soil pioneer families to Kansas, establishing fortified antislavery towns like Lawrence, Topeka, and Manhattan. Senator Stephen Douglas popular sovereignty doctrine set the prairie ablaze, transforming Kansas into a bloody ideological battleground between pro-slavery Missourians and abolitionist pioneers.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: BORDER RUFFIANS AND BEECHER'S BIBLES
Across the Missouri River, pro-slavery forces reacted with apoplectic fury. Missouri Senator David Rice Atchison mobilized a paramilitary army of Missouri frontiersmen known to history as 'Border Ruffians.' Armed with shotguns, bowie knives, and whiskey jugs, the Border Ruffians rode across the border on election days, terrorizing election judges, stuffing ballot boxes with thousands of fraudulent votes, and electing a fraudulent pro-slavery territorial legislature that enacted draconian laws making criticism of slavery a felony punishable by death. In the North, prominent abolitionist minister Henry Ward Beecher declared that a Sharps breech-loading rifle was a more persuasive moral argument against slavery than a Bible. New England societies promptly shipped thousands of state-of-the-art Sharps military rifles to Kansas Free-Staters, concealing the weapons inside wooden shipping crates labeled 'Bibles' and 'Carpentry Tools.' Both sides formed armed militias, and throughout eighteen fifty-five and early eighteen fifty-six, rival factions ambushed one another along prairie roads, burned homesteads, and turned the territory into an armed camp known in headlines across the globe as 'Bleeding Kansas.' Henry Ward Beecher congregation shipped wooden crates labeled Bibles that actually contained state-of-the-art Sharps repeating rifles, giving rise to the famous frontier term Beechers Bibles.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SACKING OF LAWRENCE
The smoldering ideological powder keg exploded in May eighteen fifty-six. A corrupt federal grand jury in Lecompton, composed entirely of pro-slavery partisans, indicted the leaders of the Free-State town of Lawrence for treason, declaring the town's two abolitionist newspapers and its fortified Free State Hotel to be illegal public nuisances. On the morning of May twenty-first, eighteen fifty-six, Douglas County Sheriff Samuel Jones led an army of eight hundred heavily armed Border Ruffians flying crimson flags that read 'Southern Rights' into the streets of Lawrence. The town's leaders, seeking to avoid a bloodbath, ordered their citizens not to resist. The pro-slavery mob went on a destructive rampage: they dragged the printing presses of the Herald of Freedom and the Kansas Free State into the streets, smashed them with sledgehammers, and threw the type into the river; they bombarded the stone Free State Hotel with cannon fire before setting it ablaze with torches, and they looted and burned private homes and shops, leaving Lawrence a smoking ruin. The pro-slavery posse ransacked the Free State Hotel with artillery and threw the printing presses of the Herald of Freedom into the Kansas River, inflaming abolitionist fury across the North.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: ENTER JOHN BROWN
Just one day after the sack of Lawrence, an equally sensational act of violence occurred on the floor of the United States Senate in Washington. South Carolina Representative Preston Brooks walked into the Senate chamber and beat Massachusetts Senator Charles Sumner unconscious with a heavy gold-headed gutta-percha cane following Sumner's speech denouncing the 'Crime Against Kansas.' News of both outrages reached an isolated, impoverished homestead along Osawatomie Creek, where fifty-six-year-old John Brown was living with four of his adult sons. Brown was an intense, devoutly religious Calvinist from Connecticut with gaunt cheeks, piercing gray eyes, and an unshakeable conviction that he was a chosen instrument of God's divine wrath against the sin of human slavery. Brown had suffered financial failures and poverty his entire life, but he possessed an iron will. Hearing of the sacking of Lawrence and the beating of Sumner, Brown flew into a cold, terrifying fury. He looked at his sons and declared: 'Something must be done to show these barbarians that we, too, have rights! Without the shedding of blood, there is no remission of sin.' John Brown was an Old Testament figure of grim, unyielding conviction, believing he was a divine instrument chosen by God to break the jaws of the wicked and overthrow human bondage by sword.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE POTTAWATOMIE MASSACRE
On the night of Saturday, May twenty-fourth, eighteen fifty-six, John Brown led a hand-picked strike squad consisting of four of his sons, a son-in-law, and two neighbors toward Pottawatomie Creek. The men were armed with revolvers, hunting rifles, and razor-sharp two-edged artillery broadswords that Brown had obtained from an Ohio Masonic lodge. Traveling under cover of pitch-black darkness, Brown's squad targeted three isolated cabins inhabited by prominent pro-slavery settlers associated with the violent border ruffian courts. Around ten o'clock, they arrived at the cabin of James Doyle, an active pro-slavery partisan. Posing as travelers, Brown knocked on the wooden door; when Doyle opened it, Brown's men dragged Doyle and his two adult sons outside into the darkness. Ignoring the frantic screams of Doyle's wife, Brown gave the signal. His sons hacked the three men to death with broadswords, splitting their skulls and severing their hands before Brown himself fired a single bullet into Doyle's forehead. Brown's squad then marched to two nearby cabins, dragging out Allen Wilkinson, a pro-slavery postmaster and legislator, and William Sherman, a violent brawler, executing both men in the same brutal fashion. By dawn, five pro-slavery men lay dead along the creek, their mutilated bodies left in the grass as a terrifying warning. Under cover of darkness along Pottawatomie Creek, Brown and his sons dragged five pro-slavery settlers from their log cabins, executing them with broadswords in a terrifying act of ideological warfare.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE GUERRILLA WAR OF 1856
The Pottawatomie Massacre sent shockwaves of sheer terror through pro-slavery ranks and instantly transformed Bleeding Kansas from sporadic political skirmishing into savage, merciless guerrilla warfare. Enraged Border Ruffians mobilized under Captain Henry Clay Pate, burning the Free-State settlement of Osawatomie. John Brown, now a wanted fugitive with a bounty on his head, embraced his role as a guerrilla commander. On June second, at the Battle of Black Jack, Brown led thirty Free-Staters in a fierce four-hour firefight against Pate's superior force, forcing Pate and thirty-two Border Ruffians to surrender—a clash regarded by many historians as the first true armed battle of the Civil War. In August, at the Battle of Osawatomie, Brown with just forty men held off an assault by four hundred pro-slavery militiamen, earning the legendary moniker 'Osawatomie Brown.' Over two hundred settlers lost their lives during eighteen fifty-six, and millions of dollars in property was destroyed before newly appointed Territorial Governor John W. Geary used federal troops to impose a fragile truce. Guerrilla skirmishes raged across eastern Kansas throughout the bloody summer of eighteen fifty-six, turning farmsteads into armed garrisons and prefiguring the national conflagration of the Civil War.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE PATH TO HARPERS FERRY AND THE UNION
Bleeding Kansas ultimately ended in a decisive political victory for the Free-State cause. Outnumbered by the relentless influx of northern homesteaders, pro-slavery forces could not maintain their fraudulent control. In eighteen fifty-nine, Kansas voters overwhelmingly ratified the anti-slavery Wyandotte Constitution, and on January twenty-ninth, eighteen sixty-one—as Southern states began seceding—Kansas was admitted to the Union as a proud free state. Meanwhile, John Brown's baptism of blood in Kansas convinced him that slavery could only be destroyed through armed slave insurrection. Three years after Pottawatomie, in October eighteen fifty-nine, Brown led his famous raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, an event that polarized the nation beyond repair and marched America straight into the Civil War. John Brown's ghost still haunts the Kansas prairie, captured in John Steuart Curry's colossal mural inside the Kansas State Capitol—depicting a towering, wild-eyed prophet holding a Bible and a rifle, reminding us that the ideals of American freedom were forged in the crucible of blood and fire.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Bleeding Kansas and the raid on Pottawatomie reveal the terrifying extremes of conviction that shattered the American republic. It shows that when compromise fails and injustice festers, the storm of history will eventually sweep all before it. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we uncover the macabre tale of the Bloody Benders of Kansas. Until then, stay curious.
